We now interpret $f{\big(}n{\big)}$ as counting the number of $n-$ tuples $\left(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\right)$ of nonnegative integers such that 

$$a_{1}1!+\cdots+a_{n}n!=n!.$$

For an upper bound on $f(n)$ I,we use the inequalities $0\leq a_{i}\leq n!/i!$ to deduce that there are at most $n!/i!+$ $1\leq2(n!/i!)$ choices for $a_{i}$ . Hence 

$$\begin{align*}f(n)&\leq2^n\frac{n!}{1!}\cdots\frac{n!}{n!}\\&=2^n2^13^2\cdots n^{n-1}\\&\leq n^{n^2/2+C_3n}e^{-n^2/4}.\end{align*}$$

For a lower bound on $f(n)$ , we note that if $0\leq a_{i}<$ $(n-1)!/i!{\mathrm{~f o r~}}i=2,\ldots,n-1$ and $a_{n}=0,$ ,then $0\leq$ $a_{2}2!+\cdots+a_{n}n!\leq n!$ , so there is a unique choice of $a_{1}$ to complete this to a solution of $a_{1}1!+\cdots+a_{n}n!=n!$ Hence 



$$\begin{align*}f(n)&\geq\frac{(n-1)!}{2!}\cdots\frac{(n-1)!}{(n-1)!}\\&=3^{1}4^{2}\cdots(n-1)^{n-3}\\&\geq n^{n^{2}/2+C_{4}n}e^{-n^{2}/4}.\end{align*}$$
